PROVISIONAL PATENT APPLICATION INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Adjustable Ergonomic Laptop Stand

INVENTION SUMMARY
Inventor Name: Jordan Lee
Title of Invention: Adjustable Ergonomic Laptop Stand
Description of Invention: A laptop stand with a spring-loaded hinge mechanism allowing continuous height and angle adjustment without tools

This sheet records basic information about the invention described above as of the date it is completed. It is an informational record only — it is not itself a patent application, and completing it does not file anything with the United States Patent and Trademark Office or create patent-pending status for Adjustable Ergonomic Laptop Stand. Whether the description above is complete and detailed enough to support any future filing is governed by the applicable statutory disclosure requirements and is determined by whoever prepares any actual application; this sheet does not evaluate or certify that sufficiency.

WHAT A PROVISIONAL APPLICATION MUST CONTAIN
Federal patent law sets out what a provisional application for patent must include, and what it doesn't. Under 35 U.S.C. § 111(b)(1), a provisional application must include a specification as prescribed by 35 U.S.C. § 112(a) — a written description of the invention — and a drawing as prescribed by 35 U.S.C. § 113, which requires a drawing only "where necessary for the understanding of the subject matter sought to be patented." The application must also be accompanied by the filing fee required by law, though the fee itself may be submitted after the filing date within a period the USPTO Director prescribes; failing to pay it within that period results in the application being regarded as abandoned. Unlike a nonprovisional application filed under 35 U.S.C. § 111(a), which must include one or more claims, 35 U.S.C. § 111(b)(2) is explicit that a claim "shall not be required in a provisional application." A provisional application describing Adjustable Ergonomic Laptop Stand — summarized in A laptop stand with a spring-loaded hinge mechanism allowing continuous height and angle adjustment without tools — would, as a factual matter, need a written specification and, where the subject matter admits of illustration, a drawing, but not a claim, to satisfy these statutory requirements.

A PROVISIONAL APPLICATION IS NEVER EXAMINED AND CANNOT ITSELF BECOME A PATENT
Federal patent law treats a provisional application differently from a regular, nonprovisional application in a fundamental way: it is never examined on its merits, and no patent can issue directly from it. 35 U.S.C. § 111(b)(8) states that the provisions of Title 35 relating to applications for patent generally apply to provisional applications, "except that provisional applications for patent shall not be subject to sections 131 and 135" — the statute governing substantive examination of an application by the Patent and Trademark Office, and the statute governing derivation proceedings between competing applicants over priority of invention. Because a provisional application is never examined under § 131, a patent can issue only from a nonprovisional application — whether a new filing or one that later claims the benefit of an earlier-filed provisional application's filing date, as described in a separate clause of this document.

PROVISIONAL FILING RECORD AND 12-MONTH REFERENCE DATE
Filing Date of Provisional Application: September 1, 2026

Under 35 U.S.C. § 111(b)(5), a provisional application is regarded as abandoned 12 months after its filing date unless a corresponding nonprovisional application claiming its benefit under 35 U.S.C. § 119(e) is filed within that period, subject to the narrow weekend-or-federal-holiday adjustment in 35 U.S.C. § 119(e)(3). Measured from the filing date entered above, that 12-month period runs to the corresponding date one year later. This record states that statutory reference point only; it does not calculate any available extension, does not track whether a nonprovisional application claiming the benefit of Adjustable Ergonomic Laptop Stand has in fact been filed, and does not indicate whether filing one would be appropriate.

THE 12-MONTH DEADLINE FOLLOWING A PROVISIONAL APPLICATION'S FILING DATE
Federal patent law fixes a firm deadline tied to a provisional application's own filing date. Under 35 U.S.C. § 111(b)(5), unless a timely request is made to treat the provisional application itself as a nonprovisional application under 35 U.S.C. § 111(a), "the provisional application shall be regarded as abandoned 12 months after the filing date of such application and shall not be subject to revival after such 12-month period." A corresponding nonprovisional application that claims the benefit of the provisional application's earlier filing date under 35 U.S.C. § 119(e) must also be filed within that same 12-month window to obtain that benefit. Federal law provides one narrow, automatic adjustment to this calendar: under 35 U.S.C. § 119(e)(3), if the day that is 12 months after the provisional application's filing date falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or federal holiday in the District of Columbia, the period is extended to the next business day. For a provisional application with a filing date of September 1, 2026, this 12-month period is measured from that date, subject to that narrow calendar adjustment.

WHAT CLAIMING THE BENEFIT OF A PROVISIONAL APPLICATION'S FILING DATE ACTUALLY DOES
The concept of a "priority date" in patent law refers to a specific statutory mechanic, not a general notion of who thought of an invention first. Under 35 U.S.C. § 119(e)(1), a nonprovisional application "shall have the same effect, as to such invention, as though filed on the date of the provisional application filed under section 111(b), if the application for patent filed under section 111(a) or section 363 is filed not later than 12 months after the date on which the provisional application was filed" — and only for the invention actually disclosed in the provisional application in the manner 35 U.S.C. § 112(a) requires, and only if the nonprovisional application contains, or is amended to contain, a specific reference to the provisional application. The provisional application itself carries no independent right of priority: 35 U.S.C. § 111(b)(7) states that "a provisional application shall not be entitled to the right of priority of any other application under section 119" or to the benefit of an earlier filing date of its own — the benefit runs only in the direction of a later-filed nonprovisional application claiming back to the provisional, not the other way. And claiming that earlier filing date doesn't lengthen the eventual patent's term: 35 U.S.C. § 154(a)(3) states that "[p]riority under section 119...shall not be taken into account in determining the term of a patent," whose term instead runs from the nonprovisional application's own filing date.

THE PUBLIC-DISCLOSURE BAR TO PATENTABILITY, AND THE ONE-YEAR GRACE PERIOD FOR THE INVENTOR'S OWN DISCLOSURES
Federal patent law can bar an invention from being patentable based on disclosures that occurred before a patent application's effective filing date — including disclosures by the inventor. Under 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(1), a person is not entitled to a patent if "the claimed invention was patented, described in a printed publication, or in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date of the claimed invention." Filing a provisional application establishes an effective filing date for this purpose, for whatever subject matter the provisional actually discloses. Federal law also provides a limited exception for the inventor's own disclosures: under 35 U.S.C. § 102(b)(1), "a disclosure made 1 year or less before the effective filing date of a claimed invention shall not be prior art to the claimed invention under subsection (a)(1)" if, among other conditions, "the disclosure was made by the inventor or joint inventor or by another who obtained the subject matter disclosed directly or indirectly from the inventor or a joint inventor." This one-year window runs backward from the effective filing date and applies only to the inventor's own qualifying disclosures (or those derived from the inventor) — it does not affect the separate, unconditional bar that can apply to a disclosure made by an unrelated third party who did not obtain the information from the inventor.

WHAT "PATENT PENDING" DOES AND DOESN'T MEAN
The phrase "patent pending" has a specific legal meaning under federal law, but that meaning is narrower than the phrase might suggest. Federal law makes it a fineable offense to mark or advertise an article with the words "patent applied for," "patent pending," or similar language "when no application for patent has been made, or if made, is not pending, for the purpose of deceiving the public" — confirming that the phrase, used honestly, indicates only that a patent application (provisional or nonprovisional) is currently on file and has not been abandoned, finally rejected, or already issued. It does not indicate that a patent will issue, and it does not itself confer any of the rights a patent confers. Under 35 U.S.C. § 154(a)(1), a patent grants its owner "a grant to the patentee, his heirs or assigns, of the right to exclude others from making, using, offering for sale, or selling the invention throughout the United States," and 35 U.S.C. § 154(a)(2) fixes the term of that grant as beginning "on the date on which the patent issues." Filing a provisional application places an application on file — and, described honestly, supports calling that status "patent pending" — but because a provisional application is never examined and cannot itself mature into a patent, patent-pending status arising from a provisional application alone does not, by itself, create any enforceable right to exclude anyone from doing anything with Adjustable Ergonomic Laptop Stand.

expectedJSON.body: Federal patent law can bar an invention from being patentable based on disclosures that occurred before a patent application's effective filing date — including disclosures by the inventor. Under 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(1), a person is not entitled to a patent if "the claimed invention was patented, described in a printed publication, or in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date of the claimed invention." Filing a provisional application establishes an effective filing date for this purpose, for whatever subject matter the provisional actually discloses. Federal law also provides a limited exception for the inventor's own disclosures: under 35 U.S.C. § 102(b)(1), "a disclosure made 1 year or less before the effective filing date of a claimed invention shall not be prior art to the claimed invention under subsection (a)(1)" if, among other conditions, "the disclosure was made by the inventor or joint inventor or by another who obtained the subject matter disclosed directly or indirectly from the inventor or a joint inventor." This one-year window runs backward from the effective filing date and applies only to the inventor's own qualifying disclosures (or those derived from the inventor) — it does not affect the separate, unconditional bar that can apply to a disclosure made by an unrelated third party who did not obtain the information from the inventor.

expectedJSON.body: The phrase "patent pending" has a specific legal meaning under federal law, but that meaning is narrower than the phrase might suggest. Federal law makes it a fineable offense to mark or advertise an article with the words "patent applied for," "patent pending," or similar language "when no application for patent has been made, or if made, is not pending, for the purpose of deceiving the public" — confirming that the phrase, used honestly, indicates only that a patent application (provisional or nonprovisional) is currently on file and has not been abandoned, finally rejected, or already issued. It does not indicate that a patent will issue, and it does not itself confer any of the rights a patent confers. Under 35 U.S.C. § 154(a)(1), a patent grants its owner "a grant to the patentee, his heirs or assigns, of the right to exclude others from making, using, offering for sale, or selling the invention throughout the United States," and 35 U.S.C. § 154(a)(2) fixes the term of that grant as beginning "on the date on which the patent issues." Filing a provisional application places an application on file — and, described honestly, supports calling that status "patent pending" — but because a provisional application is never examined and cannot itself mature into a patent, patent-pending status arising from a provisional application alone does not, by itself, create any enforceable right to exclude anyone from doing anything with Adjustable Ergonomic Laptop Stand.
